claims.claim: Christians should take on positions of power in government.

stances.original: Vel hoc te commonefaciat omnes huius saeculi potestates et dignitates non solum alienas, uerum et inimicas dei esse
stances.summary: The powers and honours of this world belong to a system that is against God. A Christian cannot wear the purple, judge, imprison or swear and stay clean, so he should not take office.
stances.quote: Let even this fact help to remind you that all the powers and dignities of this world are not only alien to, but enemies of, God
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, 1885
stances.context: Chapter 17 reports 'a dispute whether a servant of God should take the administration of any dignity or power', with Joseph and Daniel cited in favour. Tertullian grants for argument's sake that someone might hold office without sacrificing, taking oaths, 'sitting in judgment on any one's life or character', imprisoning or torturing, then adds 'if it is credible that all this is possible'. Chapter 18 answers that Christ 'shrank back from being made a king' and so gave His own an example against the pride of dignity and power. Other lines, same translator: Apology 21 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0301.htm): 'Yes, and the Cæsars too would have believed on Christ, if either the Cæsars had not been necessary for the world, or if Christians could have been Cæsars.' Apology 38: 'nor is there anything more entirely foreign to us than affairs of state' (said to show that Christians are no political club, not as a rule about office). On the Pallium 5.4 (ANF vol. 4, https://www.tertullian.org/anf/anf04/anf04-03.htm), where the philosopher's cloak speaks for him: 'I owe no duty to the forum, the election-ground, or the senate-house'. Dates: Apology 197; On Idolatry disputed (c. 196 to c. 211); On the Pallium c. 205-210. The view runs through his catholic-period works and is not a product of his later Montanism. Latin (original field) checked at https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.idololatria.shtml; Apology Latin at https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.apol.shtml ('si et Christiani potuissent esse Caesares'; 'nec ulla magis res aliena quam publica').

stances.summary: I have no wish to rule, to be rich or to command troops. A Christian turns down power and fame.
stances.quote: I do not wish to be a king; I am not anxious to be rich; I decline military command
stances.translation: J.E. Ryland, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2, 1885
stances.work: Address to the Greeks (Oratio ad Graecos)
stances.context: A personal renunciation in a list of worldly aims (riches, fame, chaplets), written c. 165-172 by a convert rejecting Greek fate and ambition. It is not an argued rule for all Christians. Tatian, a pupil of Justin, later left the Church and led the Encratites (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.28): mark him heterodox. Greek original not checked.

stances.summary: Christians turn down public office. Not to dodge duty, but to keep themselves for a higher and more needed service: leading the Church and saving people.
stances.quote: And it is not for the purpose of escaping public duties that Christians decline public offices, but that they may reserve themselves for a diviner and more necessary service in the Church of God— for the salvation of men.
stances.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, 1885
stances.context: Written c. 248, answering the pagan Celsus, who 'urges us to take office in the government of the country, if that is required for the maintenance of the laws and the support of religion' (same chapter). Origen answers that Christians belong to 'another national organization, founded by the Word of God' (the Church), and that able and modest men should be pressed to rule there. Chapters 73-74 make the parallel case for the army: Christians help the emperor by prayer, not arms. He assumes a pagan empire whose offices meant sacrifice and bloodshed, and does not discuss a Christian emperor. Some of Origen's speculative teachings were condemned in 553 (mark heterodox); this position is not among them. Greek original not checked.

stances.summary: A magistrate who wears the purple cannot be taken in for baptism. He must give up the office or be turned away.
stances.quote: A military commander or civic magistrate that wears the purple must resign or be rejected.
stances.translation: Burton Scott Easton, The Apostolic Tradition of Hippolytus, Cambridge University Press, 1934 (published by Project Gutenberg as public domain in the US; later than 1929, so check before use outside the US)
stances.context: A church order listing trades a catechumen must give up. 'The purple' marks magistrates with power over life and death. The same list says a soldier 'must be taught not to kill men and to refuse to do so if he is commanded, and to refuse to take an oath', and that a catechumen or believer who seeks to become a soldier must be rejected. The ascription to Hippolytus (c. 215) is disputed; many scholars now treat it as a composite text built up between the 2nd and 4th centuries. The Greek is lost; the text is reconstructed from Latin, Coptic, Arabic and Ethiopic versions, so original is null. In the Gutenberg HTML, superscript verse numbers sit before 'A military' and after 'rejected.'.

stances.summary: The honours of office look sweet but hide poison. The safe course is to step out of the whirl of the world and look to heaven.
stances.quote: In respect of what you regard as honours, of what you consider the fasces, what you count affluence in riches, what you think power in the camp, the glory of the purple in the magisterial office, the power of licence in the chief command — there is hidden the virus of ensnaring mischief
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, 1886
stances.work: To Donatus (Ad Donatum; Epistle 1 in the ANF numbering)
stances.context: Written c. 246, soon after his baptism, by a wealthy Carthaginian teacher of rhetoric. It is a meditation on the misery of the world, not a church rule. Section 3 recalls his fear before baptism: 'One who has felt the charm of the fasces and of civic honours shrinks from becoming a mere private and inglorious citizen.' Section 14: the one secure peace is 'for a man to withdraw from these eddies of a distracting world'. As bishop (from 248/9) he did not rule on office-holding in any text found.

stances.original: ideo dicit dominus: non potestis duobus dominis seruire, scilicet uni deo et mammonae, Christo uidelicet et Caesari, cum ipse Caesar Christi seruus nunc studeat esse, ut aliquarum gentium rex esse mereatur.
stances.summary: No one can serve two masters, Christ and Caesar. Put no homeland, honours or riches before God, and leave the world's service now, not later.
stances.quote: That is why the Lord says: You cannot serve two masters, that is, the one God and mammon, namely Christ and Caesar, even though Caesar himself is now eager to be Christ's servant, so that he may deserve to be king over some nations.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (CSEL 29, ed. W. von Hartel, 1894, p. 225)
stances.context: Written from Nola (after 395) to Crispinianus, a soldier in imperial service in Gaul. Its main target is armed service ('qui militat gladio mortis est minister': whoever serves with the sword is a servant of death), so it bears on office by extension. Section 2: 'Ideo nec affectum nec patriam nec honores nec diuitias deo praeferre debemus' (so we must put neither affection nor homeland nor public honours nor riches before God). In Letter 8 he urges the young Licentius, then seeking a career at Rome, away from marriage and 'celsos... honores' (lofty offices). Paulinus had himself been governor of Campania (c. 381) and in 394-395 gave up his senatorial life and wealth; Ambrose, Letter 58.3, imagines 'the great of the world' saying he 'should have seceded from the senate' (https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/ambrose_letters_06_letters51_60.htm). The only English version of the letters (P.G. Walsh, 1966-67) is copyrighted, so the rendering is my own. The archive.org OCR splits words at line ends ('duo- bus', 'stu- deat') and prints 'nee' for 'nec'.

stances.summary: While he lived in the imperial palace he asked God how to be saved. The answer was to flee from men, so he left the court for the desert.
stances.quote: When Abba Arsenius was in the palace, he prayed to God, and said, "O Lord, direct me how to live"; and a voice came to him, saying, "Arsenius, flee from men, and thou shalt live."
stances.translation: E.A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907 (from the Syriac of Anan-Isho)
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge, The Paradise, vol. 2)
stances.location: first saying of chapter 1 ("Of flight from men"); Arsenius 1 in the Greek alphabetical collection
stances.context: The archive.org OCR prints 'WHEN' in capitals, puts spaces inside the quotation marks and misreads one quotation mark as '11' ('flee from 11 men'); a machine check will need to allow for that. The same volume says of him: 'He lived in the world, in the palace, for forty years, in the days of Theodosius, the great king'. A personal call to leave court life, not a rule for other Christians; the saying says nothing against those who stay in office. Related monastic counsel, Poemen (saying 277 in Budge): 'Thou shalt possess no knowledge of the judge (or governor), lest, when thou hearest his words, thou perform his work' (advice to monks, so not recorded as a stance).

stances.original: Magistratus vero uno anno quo agit duumviratum, prohibendum placet ut se ab ecclesia cohibeat.
stances.person: Synod of Elvira (bishops of Spain, c. 306)
stances.summary: A Christian may serve as a town magistrate. But for his year in office he must stay away from the church.
stances.quote: It is decided that a magistrate, in the one year in which he serves as duumvir, is to be barred, so that he keeps himself away from the church.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin
stances.work: Canons of the Synod of Elvira
stances.context: The url is Hefele, A History of the Christian Councils vol. 1 (tr. W.R. Clark, 1894), p. 161, whose OCR breaks 'prohi- bendum'. Duumvirs were the two chief magistrates of a Roman town, elected for a year; the office could not be refused. Hefele explains that they had to watch over temples and preside at festivals with a pagan character, so the synod kept them from church while in office rather than forbidding the office: 'An absolute prohibition to hold this office would have given up the charge of the most important towns to pagans.' The same synod punished Christian flamens who sacrificed far more harshly (canons 2-4). Date disputed (c. 295-314). A council, not a person: evidence of the church's stance before Constantine, not a quiz result.

stances.summary: A just man may not kill, even lawfully, so he cannot be a soldier or bring a capital charge. Yet he rejoiced when Constantine took power and restored Christian worship.
stances.quote: Thus it will be neither lawful for a just man to engage in warfare, since his warfare is justice itself, nor to accuse any one of a capital charge, because it makes no difference whether you put a man to death by word, or rather by the sword, since it is the act of putting to death itself which is prohibited.
stances.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7, 1886
stances.context: Written c. 303-311, during and after the Great Persecution, by a teacher of rhetoric who had held an imperial post at Nicomedia and later tutored Constantine's son Crispus. The rule forbids the killing that Roman magistrates and soldiers did, not office as such. In On the Deaths of the Persecutors 24 (c. 315, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0705.htm) he writes: 'Constantine Augustus, having assumed the government, made it his first care to restore the Christians to the exercise of their worship and to their God'. So: no bloodshed, but a welcome for Christian rule. Latin original not checked against an edition.

stances.summary: When Christian emperors wrote to him he approved of them for worshipping Christ. He told them to rule with mercy and justice, care for the poor, and remember that Christ alone is the true King.
stances.quote: wrote an answer approving them because they worshipped Christ, and giving them counsel on things pertaining to salvation: 'not to think much of the present, but rather to remember the judgment that is coming, and to know that Christ alone was the true and Eternal King.' He begged them to be merciful and to give heed to justice and the poor.
stances.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers 2nd series vol. 4, 1892
stances.context: A Life written c. 357-362 by Athanasius, who knew him; reported speech, not Antony's own writing. The emperors are Constantine and his sons. Antony at first would not open the letters ('Do not be astonished if an emperor writes to us, for he is a man') and replied only because the monks urged him 'because the emperors were Christians'. He did not tell them to lay down power; he told them how to use it, while fleeing all public life himself.

stances.summary: It is better to be in the lowest rank with God than first beside an earthly king. Still, a Christian who serves at court and puts God first is not to be blamed.
stances.quote: for I will confess to you that I think it a better and grander thing to be in the lowest rank with God than to win the first place with an earthly king. Nevertheless I cannot blame him
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers 2nd series vol. 7, 1894
stances.work: Oration 7, Panegyric on his brother Caesarius
stances.context: Funeral speech (c. 368-369) for his brother Caesarius, a court physician who later held a treasury post in Bithynia. Gregory calls the public career 'the lower form of life', acceptable for one who 'sets greater store on God and his own salvation than on earthly lustre'. He praises Caesarius for standing firm as a Christian before Julian (sections 11-13), yet says in section 15 that he was always 'pained that his great nature should be occupied in affairs beneath it'. His own choice was withdrawal, which he calls philosophy.

stances.summary: No office on earth matches what a Christian gains by giving the world up. Yet he cheered a Christian prefect who used his power to smash a pagan shrine.
stances.quote: Can anything be more splendid than the consulate? Yet the honour lasts only for a year and when another has succeeded to the post its former occupant gives way.
stances.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers 2nd series vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Written 397 to Pammachius, a senator who became a monk; 'Today all the churches of Christ are talking of Pammachius', more than of any consul. In Letter 107.2 (c. 400, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3001107.htm) he praises Gracchus, who 'when a few years back he held the prefecture of the City, overthrow, break in pieces, and shake to pieces the grotto of Mithras'. He ranks renunciation above office but welcomes Christian power used against paganism. Weak evidence either way.

stances.summary: Power over men is given from heaven so that earthly rule may serve the kingdom of heaven. Many can live a holy life in public service, but many others can only be saved by leaving everything.
stances.quote: For there are many who are able to live a religious life even in a secular condition: but there are very many who cannot in any wise be saved with God unless they give up all things.
stances.translation: James Barmby, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers 2nd series vol. 12, 1895
stances.work: Letters (Registrum epistolarum), to the Emperor Maurice
stances.location: Book 3, Letter 65 in NPNF (III, 61 in the MGH numbering)
stances.context: Written 593 against Maurice's law barring public officials and soldiers from becoming monks. Gregory 'greatly commended' the part that barred officials from moving straight into church office, since such a man 'is not wishing to relinquish secular affairs, but to change them'. He reminds the emperor: 'For power over all men has been given from heaven to the piety of my lords to this end, that they who aspire to what is good may be helped, and that the way to heaven may be more widely open, so that an earthly kingdom may wait upon the heavenly kingdom' (the Latin is usually cited as 'ut terrestre regnum caelesti regno famuletur'; not checked against an edition). Gregory was himself prefect of Rome (c. 573) before becoming a monk. In the letter to Leander that opens his Moralia (Oxford 1844 translation, https://www.lectionarycentral.com/GregoryMoralia/Epistle.html) he regrets that 'for late and long I declined the grace of conversion' and 'thought it better to be still shrouded in the secular habit'. Pastoral Rule 1.5 blames gifted people who 'fly from' rule for their own ease, but it concerns rule in the Church.

stances.summary: Public affairs must be run well, and the statesman does real work. But the goal of every life is to know God, and that pursuit is the best life.
stances.quote: Then, in my opinion, the end both of the statesman, and of him who lives according to the law, is contemplation. It is necessary, therefore, that public affairs should be rightly managed. But to philosophize is best.
stances.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Written c. 198-203 in a chapter arguing that Plato took his laws from Moses. By 'philosophize' Clement means the Christian pursuit of the knowledge of God. In the Exhortation to the Greeks, chapter 10 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/020810.htm), he tells converts to stay in their callings: 'Has knowledge taken hold of you while engaged in military service? Listen to the commander, who orders what is right.' He never directly discusses Christians holding Roman office. Weak evidence.

stances.original: De praesidibus qui fideles ad praesidatum prosiliunt, ita placuit ut, com promoti fuerint, litteras accipiant ecclesiasticas communicatorias, ita tamen ut, in quibuscumque locis gesserint, ab episcopo eiusdem loci cura illis agatur, et com coeperint contra disciplinam agere, tunc demum a communione excludantur. Similiter et de his qui rem publicam agere volunt.
stances.summary: Christians who become provincial governors stay in communion. The local bishop keeps watch over them, and they are cut off only if they act against church discipline.
stances.quote: Concerning believers who rise to become provincial governors, it was decided that when they are promoted they should receive church letters of communion. Wherever they serve, the bishop of that place is to take care of them, and only if they begin to act against discipline are they to be excluded from communion. The same applies to those who wish to hold public office.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin
stances.work: Canons of the Council of Arles
stances.location: canon 7 in Hefele (canon 6 in the list at the url)
stances.context: Held under Constantine in 314. Hefele (A History of the Christian Councils vol. 1, tr. W.R. Clark, 1894, https://archive.org/download/historyofchristi00hefe/historyofchristi00hefe_djvu.txt) reads it as relaxing Elvira canon 56 now that the emperor was Christian: 'It was necessary that, under a Christian emperor and altered circumstances, the ancient rigour should be relaxed'. 'Com' is the manuscript spelling of 'cum'. 'Rem publicam agere' covers civic office in general. Permission with oversight rather than exhortation. A council, not a person.

stances.summary: A Christian emperor is God's friend and rules as His deputy on earth. When Christians take the throne, the prophecy that the saints will take the kingdom comes true.
stances.quote: by the appointment of the Cæsars, fulfills the predictions of the holy prophets, according to what they uttered ages before: And the saints of the Most High shall take the kingdom.
stances.translation: Ernest Cushing Richardson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers 2nd series vol. 1, 1890
stances.work: Oration in Praise of Constantine (Tricennial Oration)
stances.context: Delivered 335-336 for Constantine's thirtieth year. The subject of the sentence is Constantine appointing his sons as Caesars; the quotation is Daniel 7:18. Life of Constantine 2.44 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/25022.htm) praises him because 'he sent governors to the several provinces, mostly such as were devoted to the saving faith'. Church History 8.1.2 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/250108.htm) records that even before the Great Persecution rulers 'committed to them the government of provinces' and excused them from sacrificing. The fullest early voice for Christian rule; often criticised as a flatterer, and his theology was suspected of Arian leanings. Not in the candidate pool, but a sharp foil to Tertullian's 'if Christians could have been Cæsars'.

stances.summary: Godly people do not enjoy office, and you have avoided it. But God wants this district run justly, so take the post, treat rich and poor alike, and God will see.
stances.quote: But it has seemed good to the Lord that the district of Ibora should not be under the power of hucksters, nor be turned into a mere slave market. It is His will that every individual in it should be enrolled, as is right. Do you therefore accept this responsibility? It is vexatious, I know, but it is one which may bring you the approbation of God.
stances.translation: Blomfield Jackson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers 2nd series vol. 8, 1895
stances.context: Written as bishop of Caesarea (370-379) to a tax assessor who disliked public work and had 'voluntarily withdrawn from even high office in the State'. Basil opens: 'It is an old saying that those who are anxious to lead a pious life do not throw themselves with pleasure into office.' He compares magistrates to physicians who 'get trouble for themselves out of other people's calamities', then urges him to serve: 'Neither fawn upon the great and powerful, nor despise the poor and needy.' Reluctant office for justice's sake, not ambition. Greek original not checked.

stances.original: Vides igitur quid auctoritas tribuat, quid suadeat misericordia. Excusationem habebis, si feceris: laudem, si non feceris.
stances.summary: A Christian judge may lawfully use the sword the law gives him, and the Church will not refuse him Communion. But he is praised if he spares life.
stances.quote: You see therefore both what power your commission gives you, and also whither mercy would lead you; you will be excused if you do it, and praised if you do it not.
stances.translation: Library of the Fathers, The Letters of S. Ambrose, revised by H. Walford, Oxford 1881
stances.context: Studius, a Christian judge, asked whether he might pass death sentences. Ambrose cites Romans 13:4 and says that some 'out of the pale of the Church' (the Benedictine editors think the Novatianists) refuse Communion to judges who have passed sentence of death, while the Church does not. He takes the Christian magistrate for granted; his hesitation is about bloodshed. Ambrose had himself been governor of Aemilia-Liguria before his sudden election as bishop in 374. His Sermon against Auxentius 36 (same page) puts the Christian emperor inside the Church: 'For the Emperor is within the Church, not over the Church; a good Emperor seeks the aid of the Church, he does not reject it'. Latin (original field) checked at https://la.wikisource.org/wiki/Epistolarum_classis_I_(Ambrosius)/3 (letter 25, AMBROSIUS STUDIO).

stances.original: In his tenebris uitae socialis sedebit iudex ille sapiens an non audebit? Sedebit plane. Constringit enim eum et ad hoc officium pertrahit humana societas, quam deserere nefas ducit.
stances.summary: Judging is grim work in a dark world. But a wise Christian will still take the judge's seat, because human society needs him and it would be wicked to abandon it.
stances.quote: If such darkness shrouds social life, will a wise judge take his seat on the bench or no? Beyond question he will. For human society, which he thinks it a wickedness to abandon, constrains him and compels him to this duty.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers 1st series vol. 2, 1887
stances.context: Written c. 426. The same chapter mourns that the judge must use torture and may condemn the innocent; a pious judge 'would cry to God From my necessities deliver me'. City of God 19.19 gives the balance: 'it is unseemly to covet the high position requisite for governing the people', but 'If no one imposes this burden upon us, we are free to sift and contemplate truth; but if it be laid upon us, we are necessitated for love's sake to undertake it.' City of God 5.24 calls Christian emperors happy 'if they rule justly' (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120105.htm). Letter 138.15 (412, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1102138.htm) dares critics to produce 'such kings, such judges' as Christ's teaching forms. Letter 220.3 (427, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1102220.htm) reminds Count Boniface that Augustine and Alypius talked him out of leaving 'all the public business in which you were engaged' for a monastery, for the sake of the service his post might render 'to the churches of Christ'. Letter 189.4, also to Boniface: 'Do not think that it is impossible for any one to please God while engaged in active military service.' No change of mind here; his known change of mind (on using state force against the Donatists) is a separate question. Latin (original field) checked at https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/augustine/civ19.shtml, which reads 'an non audebit' where some editions have 'an non sedebit'.

stances.original: Tu eiusdem uiri ore hanc sapientibus capessendae rei publicae necessariam causam esse monuisti, ne improbis flagitiosisque ciuibus urbium relicta gubernacula pestem bonis ac perniciem ferrent. Hanc igitur auctoritatem secutus quod a te inter secreta otia didiceram transferre in actum publicae amministrationis optaui.
stances.summary: Wise and good people must take up government. If they leave it to scoundrels, the good will suffer, so I entered public office for the common good.
stances.quote: By his mouth likewise thou didst point out this imperative reason why philosophers should enter public life, to wit, lest, if the reins of government be left to unprincipled and profligate citizens, trouble and destruction should come upon the good. Following these precepts, I have tried to apply in the business of public administration the principles which I learnt from thee in leisured seclusion.
stances.translation: H.R. James, 1897 (Project Gutenberg text)
stances.context: Written c. 524 in prison before his execution. Boethius was consul (510) and master of offices under Theoderic; he says he 'brought to my duties no aim but zeal for the public good' and tells how he blocked officials who preyed on the weak. The argument is Plato's, spoken to Lady Philosophy; the Consolation never names Christ, but Boethius wrote Christian theological treatises and is venerated as a martyr at Pavia. The plain-text url has line breaks inside the quotation. Latin (original field) checked at https://faculty.georgetown.edu/jod/boethius/jkok/1p4_t.htm, where the section number 7 stands between the two sentences.

splits_fathers: Real voices on both sides, and the line runs mostly through time. Before Constantine (to c. 313) the recorded voices lean against: Tertullian, Origen, the Apostolic Tradition, Tatian and Cyprian treat office as tied to idolatry, oaths and bloodshed, and the Synod of Elvira keeps town magistrates out of church for their year. Even then Christians did hold office (Eusebius, Church History 8.1.2; Elvira and Arles assume it), and Tertullian reports a live 'dispute' with Joseph and Daniel cited on the other side. After Constantine the balance swings: the Council of Arles keeps Christian governors in communion; Eusebius hails Christian rule; Basil, Ambrose and Augustine accept or urge office for justice's sake; Boethius takes it on Plato's grounds; Gregory the Great calls imperial power the servant of the heavenly kingdom. A strong ascetic current runs alongside (Arsenius, Paulinus, Gregory of Nazianzus, Jerome, and Gregory's own regrets) that ranks leaving the world above office without forbidding office to others. The commonest late view: do not seek power, accept it if it is laid on you, rule justly, and be slow to shed blood.
splits_people_today: As worded, most people today would agree, Christian or not: few object to a Christian running for office, and most churchgoing Christians would say believers should serve. Dissent is real but smaller: Anabaptist traditions (Amish, many Old Order Mennonites) have historically refused magistracy (the Schleitheim Confession of 1527, article 6, like Tertullian, points to Christ refusing to be made king); Jehovah's Witnesses stay out of politics altogether; some Christians hold that seeking power corrupts the Church; and many secular people distrust Christians who seek power in order to pass faith-based laws, so 'Christian nationalism' splits people sharply. To split players more evenly, frame a trade-off rather than a permission: 'A serious Christian should stay out of politics and power', 'You cannot hold real power and keep clean hands', or 'Good people have a duty to take power so bad people don't get it'. The Fathers split cleanly on exactly those framings: Tertullian and Origen on purity and a higher calling, Basil, Augustine and Boethius on duty.

misattributions.line: Nothing is more foreign to us than politics.
misattributions.truth: A loose modern paraphrase of Apology 38.3 ('nec ulla magis res aliena quam publica'; Thelwall: 'nor is there anything more entirely foreign to us than affairs of state'). In context it argues that Christians are no political club or faction, not that they may not hold office; his case against office is in On Idolatry 17-18.

misattributions.line: The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church.
misattributions.truth: Paraphrase. Apology 50.13 reads 'semen est sanguis Christianorum' (Thelwall: 'the blood of Christians is seed'). Genuine in sense, not verbatim.

misattributions.line: A military commander or civic magistrate that wears the purple must resign or be rejected.
misattributions.truth: The line is genuine to the church order called the Apostolic Tradition, but its ascription to Hippolytus (c. 215) is disputed and the text is composite. Safer on screen: 'an early church order (the Apostolic Tradition)'.

notes: 1. Chrysostom: no clear first-hand statement on this claim was found in the NPNF homilies (Matthew, John, Acts, Romans, 1-2 Corinthians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 1-2 Timothy, Hebrews, On the Statues were all searched). Homily 23 on Romans treats rulers as God's institution and says subjects should honour them 'much more ... now they are believers'. His early treatise 'A Comparison between a King and a Monk' (Greek in Migne PG 47) argues the monk is the truer king, but its only English translation (D.G. Hunter, 1988) is copyrighted and the Greek was not reachable here; do not place Chrysostom on this claim without an own rendering from that Greek. 2. Poemen: his counsel to avoid judges and governors is advice to monks, and he told a judge who held his nephew to 'Examine and consider his case according to the Law' (Budge saying 265), accepting the judge's role; not recorded as a stance. 3. Novatian: Ambrose (Letter 25.2) reports that some outside the Church refused Communion to judges who passed death sentences; the Benedictine editors identify them as Novatianists. That is a report about a later group, not Novatian's own words, so it cannot be used for Novatian. 4. Justin (1 Apology 17) and Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.24) teach obedience to rulers set by God; neither says whether Christians should hold office. 5. Donatus of Carthage, the schismatic bishop, is reported by Optatus (Against the Donatists 3.3, tr. O.R. Vassall-Phillips 1917, https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/optatus_03_book3.htm) as saying 'What has the Emperor to do with the Church?'; Optatus answers 'For the State is not in the Church, but the Church is in the State'. That is a church-and-state question, not office-holding. 6. Military service is a neighbouring question and deserves its own claim: Apostolic Tradition 16, Origen Against Celsus 8.73, Lactantius Divine Institutes 6.20, Paulinus Letter 25, Augustine Letters 189 and 220, and Martin of Tours all bear on it. Several texts above (Apostolic Tradition, Lactantius, Ambrose) object to the bloodshed of office more than to office itself; a quiz statement about the death penalty or judging would sort them more sharply. 7. Pool members with nothing found on this claim: Ignatius, Irenaeus, Perpetua, Novatian, Athanasius (own voice), Ephrem, Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa, Macrina, Syncletica, Moses the Black, Poemen (see 2), Evagrius, Pelagius, John Cassian, Martin (soldiering only), Benedict, John Climacus, Isaac the Syrian, John Chrysostom (see 1). 8. Councils (Elvira, Arles) and non-pool figures (Tatian, Eusebius) are recorded as evidence, not as quiz results. 9. Best result pairings: Tertullian's 'if Christians could have been Cæsars' against Eusebius's 'the saints of the Most High shall take the kingdom'; Origen ('Christians decline public offices') against Basil ('Do you therefore accept this responsibility?'); Augustine's 'Beyond question he will' for the judge's seat.
